query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Post-solidification thermal treatment in a controlled low oxygen partial pressure atmosphere forms a thin, ductile interfacial film along the lamellar colony boundaries, thereby enhancing interface cohesion and simultaneously improving both tensile strength and ductility compared to the untreated eutectic HEA.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase (fcc/B2) lamellar colonies where numerous internal boundaries act as microcrack nucleation sites under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Apply a targeted post-solidification thermal treatment in an atmosphere with a controlled (low) oxygen partial pressure.
generation.conditions: Treatment is conducted after casting and before mechanical testing, with room-temperature tensile deformation used to assess performance. The atmosphere and thermal treatment schedule must be precisely controlled to promote the formation of an interfacial film without altering the primary phase chemistries.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, ductile interfacial film (or controlled elemental segregation) residing along the internal boundaries of the lamellar colonies.
generation.mechanism: The induced interfacial film reinforces the cohesion of the lamellar boundaries, mitigating microcrack initiation and propagation. This reduces stress concentrations and delays failure, resulting in a simultaneous improvement in both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples receiving the thermal treatment will exhibit both a higher ultimate tensile strength and increased elongation (ductility) at room temperature relative to the untreated (as-cast) baseline.
generation.baseline: The conventional as-cast eutectic HEA with dual-phase lamellar colonies, which typically shows high strength but limited ductility due to microcrack initiation along weak internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under room-temperature tensile deformation and requires that the treatment parameters (temperature, duration, controlled low oxygen atmosphere) be optimized. The effect may not hold if the treatment conditions are significantly altered or performed at different temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement in strength and ductility is uncertain and may depend sensitively on the specific thermal parameters and oxygen level; optimization is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set undergoes the specified post-solidification thermal treatment under controlled low oxygen partial pressure, and the control set remains untreated. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests to measure tensile strength and elongation. Use microscopy (e.g., TEM or SEM) to verify the formation of the ductile interfacial film along lamellar boundaries.
measurements: Microstructural characterization of interfacial regions (film presence, thickness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the untreated samples, or if the expected ductile interfacial film is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. decision.trend: Earlier work on eutectic high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) with lamellar fcc/B2 architectures (e.g., PMC4145285) showed that conventional casting routes generate fine dual‐phase lamellar colonies that impart high strength but are prone to microcrack initiation along the multitude of internal interfaces. Researchers then attempted thermomechanical processing (such as cold rolling and subsequent annealing) and various microstructural design strategies to alter phase volume fractions and refine interlamellar spacing. While these interventions have improved strength, they did so mainly at the expense of ductility, because the internal boundaries still remain weak points susceptible to crack initiation under room‐temperature tensile loading.
decision.unsolved: The central unsolved issue is how to simultaneously improve the intrinsic strength of the bulk phases and, crucially, enhance the cohesion and toughness of the multiple internal interfaces within the dual-phase lamellar colonies so as to prevent microcrack nucleation and propagation under room‐temperature tensile deformation.
decision.lever: Apply a targeted post-solidification thermal treatment under a controlled atmosphere (e.g., with a low, controlled oxygen partial pressure) designed to induce a thin, ductile interfacial film (or controlled segregations) along the lamellar colony boundaries.
decision.why: This strategy follows from the observed trend that bulk processing and microstructure modifications (via processing or compositional adjustments) primarily altered the strength without adequately addressing the inherent brittleness at the interfaces. By engineering the internal boundaries themselves—improving their cohesion without changing the primary phase chemistries—the intervention is expected to arrest microcrack initiation, thereby simultaneously enhancing both strength and ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline. Prior evidence on interface‐controlled toughening in multi-phase alloys supports the concept that reinforcing or subtly modifying interface chemistry and structure can improve damage tolerance. An experiment comparing room‐temperature tensile properties of samples with and without the post‐processing interface treatment would allow falsification if no improvement in ductility (with maintained or improved strength) is observed under defined temperature and atmosphere conditions.
